title: Pretraining
plain_meaning: Pretraining is the broad learning phase where a model predicts the next token (a token is a chunk of text, usually a word or a word-piece) across a huge corpus and absorbs language, facts, patterns, styles, and many weak forms of reasoning.
first_principles: The model is not directly taught to be helpful or to solve tasks. It is repeatedly asked: given this context, what token is likely next? To reduce error, it must build internal representations of grammar, concepts, procedures, facts, code, mathematical patterns, and the distribution of human-written reasoning.
example: If the text says 'To solve 2x + 3 = 7, subtract 3 from both sides...', the model learns that algebra explanations often continue with a transformation step. Across many examples, this creates latent algebraic behavior.
why_it_matters: Most later alignment, reasoning, RL, and agentic behavior sits on top of pretraining. If the base model does not already contain useful representations, post-training has little to elicit.
misunderstanding: Pretraining is not just memorization. It includes memorization, but the useful part is compression: learning reusable structure that generalizes across contexts.

title: Base Model Capability
plain_meaning: A base model is often more capable than one ordinary sample suggests because its probability distribution contains many possible reasoning paths, including rare good ones.
first_principles: A language model defines a probability distribution over completions — a ranked spread of possible answers, each with its own likelihood. One answer is only one draw from that distribution. Capability is therefore not just what appears in the first sample; it also includes what can be found through repeated sampling, search, or better decoding.
example: A base model may answer a math problem incorrectly on its first attempt, but among 100 attempts it may produce a fully correct solution. The skill was present, but not reliably selected.
why_it_matters: This explains why pass@k, power sampling, best-of-k, and test-time compute can make base models look much stronger without changing weights.
misunderstanding: A bad first answer does not prove the model lacks the ability. It may prove that the default sampling method failed to elicit the ability.

title: Sampling
plain_meaning: Sampling is the process of choosing tokens from the model's probability distribution during generation.
first_principles: At each step, the model gives probabilities for possible next tokens. Decoding rules decide whether to pick the most likely token, sample randomly, sharpen the distribution, truncate low-probability tokens, or search across multiple possible futures.
example: With high temperature, the model may explore more unusual solution paths. With low temperature, it becomes more predictable but may get stuck in a common flawed path.
why_it_matters: Reasoning quality depends heavily on how the model is sampled. Different sampling methods trade off reliability, diversity, cost, and exploration.
misunderstanding: Sampling is not a cosmetic output setting. For reasoning tasks, sampling can determine which internal strategy the model follows.

title: Test-Time Compute
plain_meaning: Test-time compute means spending more computation when answering a question, without changing the model weights.
first_principles: If a model has a distribution containing both weak and strong paths, extra runtime computation can search that distribution, generate multiple candidates, revise intermediate work, or verify outputs. The model stays fixed, but the inference procedure becomes stronger.
example: Instead of asking for one answer to a coding problem, generate 50 programs, run unit tests, and keep the one that passes.
why_it_matters: This is central to reasoning models and agents because many hard tasks are not solved by one forward pass. They require search, checking, retries, and budget allocation.
misunderstanding: Test-time compute is not free intelligence. It only helps when there is a way to select better outputs or use feedback.

title: Supervised Finetuning
plain_meaning: Supervised finetuning trains a model on examples of desired input-output behavior.
first_principles: After pretraining learns broad representations, SFT changes how the model responds to a prompt. It shows the model what kind of answer should follow: concise answer, chain of reasoning, tool call, JSON format, safety refusal, or domain-specific response.
example: A dataset of customer support questions and ideal responses teaches the model to answer in the company's support style.
why_it_matters: SFT is the easiest way to teach format, style, task behavior, and teacher-model reasoning traces. Distillation is often implemented as SFT on synthetic outputs from a stronger model.
misunderstanding: SFT is not only about making a model polite. It can transfer procedural traces and sometimes install reasoning patterns the base model did not naturally use.

title: Distillation
plain_meaning: Distillation trains one model to imitate another model, usually to transfer capability into a cheaper, smaller, or more specialized model.
first_principles: A teacher model produces outputs, reasoning traces, labels, preferences, or demonstrations. A student model trains on those artifacts. The student may learn behavior that would be expensive to discover from raw data alone.
example: A strong reasoning model solves many math problems step by step. A smaller model is finetuned on those solutions and becomes much better at similar math tasks.
why_it_matters: Distillation can expand a student's practical reasoning boundary more than RL alone because it supplies explicit high-quality worked solutions rather than only a final right-or-wrong score.
misunderstanding: Distillation is not always about making a smaller clone. A larger student can also improve by learning from generated data from a different teacher.

title: RLHF
plain_meaning: RLHF means reinforcement learning from human feedback, usually used to align model outputs with human preferences.
first_principles: Humans compare or rate model outputs. A reward model learns those preferences. The language model is then optimized to produce outputs the reward model scores highly.
example: Given two answers, humans prefer the answer that is more helpful and less evasive. The model is trained to increase the probability of answers like that.
why_it_matters: RLHF made chat models more usable, but it can also produce over-optimization, sycophancy (telling people what they want to hear), mode collapse (falling back on a few safe responses), or responses that look good to the reward model without being truly better.
misunderstanding: RLHF is not the same as RLVR. RLHF uses human preference signals; RLVR uses automatically checkable correctness signals.

title: RLVR
plain_meaning: RLVR is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: the model gets rewarded when an answer can be automatically checked as correct.
first_principles: For tasks like math, code, theorem proving, and tool use, correctness can often be checked by rules, tests, execution, or exact answers. RLVR uses those checks as reward signals to increase the probability of successful reasoning trajectories (a trajectory is one full attempt, from first step to final answer).
example: A model generates code. Unit tests pass or fail. Passing trajectories are reinforced; failing trajectories are discouraged.
why_it_matters: RLVR is central to modern reasoning models because it gives scalable feedback without requiring humans to label every step.
misunderstanding: RLVR does not necessarily create brand-new reasoning machinery. It may mostly make successful existing paths more likely.

title: GRPO
plain_meaning: GRPO is a group-relative RL method that compares multiple answers to the same prompt and rewards answers that are better than the group average.
first_principles: Instead of needing a separate 'critic' model — a helper trained to predict how good an answer will turn out — GRPO samples a group of completions for one problem, scores them, and uses relative performance inside the group as the learning signal.
example: For one math problem, the model generates eight answers. Three are correct and five are wrong. The correct ones are reinforced relative to the wrong ones.
why_it_matters: GRPO helped make RLVR practical for reasoning because it reduces infrastructure complexity and uses the natural contrast among sampled attempts.
misunderstanding: GRPO does not learn from a problem if every sampled answer is equally good or equally bad. The useful signal comes from contrast.

title: DAPO
plain_meaning: DAPO is a refinement of group-relative RL that focuses training on prompts where the sampled group contains both successes and failures, while also managing exploration and response length.
first_principles: RL needs contrast. If all samples are wrong, the model does not know what worked. If all samples are correct, the task is too easy. DAPO keeps the model in the useful middle region where reward differences reveal which reasoning paths should be reinforced.
example: If eight attempts produce four correct and four wrong answers, DAPO trains on that prompt. If all eight are wrong or all eight are correct, it may skip or downweight the prompt.
why_it_matters: DAPO directly addresses the practical problem of sparse or uninformative rewards in RLVR. It is a curriculum and filtering idea as much as an optimizer detail.
misunderstanding: DAPO is not magic reasoning. It is a way to choose training examples where RL has useful information.

title: Pass@1 And Pass@k
plain_meaning: Pass@1 measures whether the first answer is correct. Pass@k measures whether at least one of k sampled answers is correct.
first_principles: Single-shot accuracy measures reliability under one draw. Multi-shot accuracy measures whether the model's distribution contains a correct solution somewhere within repeated attempts.
example: A model with 40% pass@1 but 90% pass@100 is unreliable but capable. A model with 70% pass@1 and 75% pass@100 is reliable but less diverse.
why_it_matters: The gap between pass@1 and pass@k reveals whether training improved reliability, expanded capability, or collapsed diversity.
misunderstanding: Higher pass@1 does not always mean the model has a broader reasoning boundary. It may simply sample a narrower set of good common paths.

title: Diversity Collapse
plain_meaning: Diversity collapse happens when training makes a model repeat a narrower set of output patterns, even if those patterns are often good.
first_principles: RL shifts probability toward rewarded trajectories — it makes those answers more likely to be produced. If the reward does not explicitly preserve variety, the model may over-concentrate on common winning strategies and suppress rare but useful alternatives.
example: After RL, a model may solve common algebra problems more reliably but stop trying unusual proof strategies that occasionally solved hard problems.
why_it_matters: This explains why RL models can improve pass@1 while hurting pass@k. It also matters for creative, open-ended, and out-of-distribution tasks (inputs unlike anything seen in training).
misunderstanding: Collapse is not always bad. For safety or routine tasks, narrowing the output distribution can be useful. The problem is losing valuable rare reasoning paths.

title: Reasoning Boundary
plain_meaning: The reasoning boundary is the set of problems a model can solve at least sometimes under some sampling or inference procedure.
first_principles: A model's practical ability has two parts: what solutions exist in its distribution and how often those solutions are sampled. RL can increase sampling frequency without necessarily expanding the set of possible solutions.
example: If a base model can solve a problem once in 500 attempts, that problem is inside its broad boundary but outside its reliable one-shot behavior.
why_it_matters: This concept separates reliability from capability. It helps interpret papers claiming that RL mostly elicits existing reasoning rather than creating new reasoning.
misunderstanding: The boundary is not identical to normal benchmark accuracy. Benchmark accuracy usually measures only a narrow inference setup.

title: Latent Reasoning
plain_meaning: Latent reasoning means reasoning behavior that the base model can produce but does not reliably expose under ordinary prompting or decoding.
first_principles: Pretraining can install many partial algorithms and reasoning traces. These behaviors may live as low-probability paths. Post-training, prompting, search, or sampling can make them easier to access.
example: A base model may rarely generate a correct backtracking strategy. A reasoning-tuned model may use backtracking frequently at the right time.
why_it_matters: It explains why inference-time methods and RL can produce large apparent gains without necessarily adding new knowledge.
misunderstanding: Latent does not mean fake. A low-probability skill can still be a real skill if the model can execute it coherently.

title: Mechanisms Versus Heuristics
plain_meaning: Mechanisms are reasoning moves the model can perform; heuristics decide when to use them.
first_principles: A model may already contain mechanisms like calculation, restatement, checking, decomposition, and backtracking. Training may primarily improve the internal decision (the control policy) about when to activate these mechanisms.
example: The model already knows how to verify an equation, but RL teaches it to verify before finalizing the answer on math problems.
why_it_matters: This distinction clarifies claims that base models know how to reason while thinking models learn when to reason.
misunderstanding: A behavior becoming more frequent after RL does not prove the mechanism was newly created by RL.

title: Process Rewards Versus Outcome Rewards
plain_meaning: Outcome rewards score the final answer. Process rewards score intermediate reasoning steps.
first_principles: Many wrong solutions look plausible until the end, and some correct answers come from invalid reasoning. Outcome rewards are cheap when final correctness is checkable, but process rewards can provide denser guidance about where reasoning went right or wrong.
example: For a math proof, an outcome reward checks the final answer. A process reward checks each algebraic transformation.
why_it_matters: Process rewards can reduce error propagation and improve training signal density, but they are harder to build and easier to miscalibrate.
misunderstanding: A process reward is not automatically more truthful. A bad process judge can reward polished but invalid reasoning.

title: Verifiers
plain_meaning: A verifier is a system that checks whether an answer, step, action, or trajectory is correct or acceptable.
first_principles: Generation creates candidates; verification selects among them or turns them into training signal. The verifier can be symbolic, executable, rule-based, learned, or another language model.
example: Unit tests verify code. A theorem checker verifies a proof. A rubric-based judge checks whether a support answer follows policy.
why_it_matters: Verifiers are the bridge between sampling and learning. Without verification, more samples may just produce more noise.
misunderstanding: An LLM judge is not automatically a reliable verifier. It needs calibration, adversarial testing, and fallback paths.

title: Data Progress
plain_meaning: Data progress means model improvement caused by better data, not necessarily by better architecture or optimizer algorithms.
first_principles: Training teaches the model the distribution it sees. If the data shifts from noisy web text to expert demonstrations, synthetic reasoning traces, code, math, and realistic task environments, the learned behavior shifts toward the capabilities people measure.
example: A model trained on curated math and code examples can outperform a similarly sized model trained mostly on generic web text.
why_it_matters: Many gains attributed to algorithmic progress may actually come from data curation, data synthesis, filtering, distillation, and benchmark-aligned task design.
misunderstanding: Data progress is not less technical than algorithm progress. Designing data pipelines, verifiers, and task environments is a core engineering challenge.

title: Synthetic Data
plain_meaning: Synthetic data is training or evaluation data generated programmatically, often by another model.
first_principles: If high-quality real examples are scarce, a model or simulator can generate prompts, answers, reasoning traces, unit tests, tool trajectories, or adversarial cases. The hard part is verifying that generated data is useful and not merely fluent.
example: A strong model generates 100,000 coding problems, solutions, and unit tests. Only solutions that pass tests are kept for training.
why_it_matters: Synthetic data enables scale in post-training, but it can amplify bias, cause contamination, or teach imitation without real capability if not verified.
misunderstanding: Synthetic data is not automatically low quality. Verified synthetic data can be extremely valuable; unverified synthetic data can be harmful.

title: Mid-Training
plain_meaning: Mid-training is an intermediate training phase between broad pretraining and final post-training, often used to specialize the model toward important domains or long-context behavior.
first_principles: Pretraining gives general capability. Final post-training shapes interaction behavior. Mid-training changes the base distribution with targeted data such as code, math, multilingual data, long-context documents, or domain corpora before alignment and RL.
example: A model is pretrained on broad web text, then mid-trained on high-quality code and math, then instruction-tuned and RL-trained.
why_it_matters: Mid-training is one reason modern models can improve substantially without obvious architectural changes.
misunderstanding: Mid-training is not just more pretraining. Its data mix and objective are chosen to move the model toward desired capabilities.

title: Mixture Of Experts
plain_meaning: MoE models contain many expert subnetworks but activate only a subset for each token.
first_principles: Dense models spend compute through the whole network for every token. MoE separates total capacity from active compute: the model can have many parameters, but the router selects a few experts per token.
example: A model may have hundreds of experts, but for a coding token it routes through code-specialized experts while using only a small fraction of total parameters.
why_it_matters: MoE increases capacity per unit of inference compute, but introduces routing instability, load balancing problems, and expert specialization questions.
misunderstanding: A 600B-parameter MoE model does not necessarily use 600B parameters of compute for each token.

title: Expert Balancing
plain_meaning: Expert balancing keeps an MoE model from overusing a few experts while ignoring others.
first_principles: If the router always chooses the same experts, unused experts do not learn well and busy experts become bottlenecks. Balancing methods encourage healthier distribution of tokens across experts.
example: During training, a bias or auxiliary objective can push the router away from overloaded experts and toward underused ones.
why_it_matters: Poor balancing wastes capacity and can destabilize reasoning because similar prompts may route through inconsistent expert paths.
misunderstanding: Expert balancing is not only a hardware efficiency trick. It affects what experts learn and how stable routing becomes.

title: QK-Norm
plain_meaning: QK-norm normalizes query and key vectors in attention to improve training stability.
first_principles: Attention scores come from interactions between query and key vectors. If their magnitudes become unstable, attention can become too sharp, too noisy, or prone to training spikes. Normalization controls the scale of those interactions.
example: Instead of letting query-key dot products grow without control, qk-norm keeps the attention comparison in a more stable range.
why_it_matters: Stable attention is especially important for large models, long contexts, and MoE systems where instability can compound.
misunderstanding: QK-norm is not a reasoning method by itself. It is an architectural stabilization method that can support better reasoning indirectly.

title: DeepSeek MLA
plain_meaning: MLA, or Multi-Head Latent Attention, compresses attention key-value information into latent representations to make long-context inference more efficient.
first_principles: Long context is expensive largely because models must store and read key-value cache entries for many tokens. MLA reduces that memory burden by representing key-value information more compactly while preserving useful attention behavior.
example: A model analyzing a long repository or research corpus can keep more context available without KV-cache costs exploding as quickly.
why_it_matters: MLA is one of the long-context unlockers that changes what tasks are practical at inference time.
misunderstanding: MLA does not make attention free. It changes the memory and compute tradeoff so long context becomes more practical.

title: Muon Optimizer
plain_meaning: Muon is an optimizer family explored as an alternative or complement to AdamW for more efficient neural network training.
first_principles: Optimizers decide how parameter updates are shaped from gradients. Matrix-aware or orthogonalized update rules can sometimes move weights through parameter space more efficiently or stably than standard elementwise adaptive methods.
example: For certain transformer components, Muon-style updates may produce better training progress for the same compute budget.
why_it_matters: If robust at scale, optimizer improvements can be real algorithmic efficiency gains rather than only data or hardware progress.
misunderstanding: An optimizer gain in one setting does not automatically translate to all frontier training runs. Scale, architecture, and implementation details matter.

title: Agentic Evaluations
plain_meaning: Agentic evaluations test systems that act over many steps using tools, memory, planning, and feedback.
first_principles: A one-question benchmark measures static answer quality. Agentic tasks measure whether the system can preserve goals, choose actions, use tools correctly, recover from errors, and complete long-horizon work.
example: Instead of asking for a code snippet, an agentic evaluation asks the model to inspect a repository, modify files, run tests, debug failures, and finish the task.
why_it_matters: Modern AI systems increasingly fail or succeed as workflows, not as single messages. Evaluation must measure the whole trajectory.
misunderstanding: Agentic evaluation is not just a longer prompt. It requires state, tools, success criteria, and failure analysis.

title: Continual Learning
plain_meaning: Continual learning is the ability of a deployed system to improve from ongoing experience without forgetting or corrupting previous capabilities.
first_principles: Humans learn from tasks while doing them. Current LLM agents mostly use fixed weights plus temporary context or external memory. Turning experience into durable, reliable improvement is difficult because updates can overfit, conflict, leak data, or degrade older behavior.
example: A coding agent repeatedly sees the same project conventions. Continual learning would let it internalize those conventions safely instead of rediscovering them every session.
why_it_matters: Self-improving agents need more than test-time retries. They need mechanisms for storing, validating, and reusing lessons across tasks.
misunderstanding: Adding memory is not the same as continual learning. Memory retrieves past facts; continual learning changes future behavior in a validated way.

title: Power Sampling
plain_meaning: Power sampling is an inference-time method that sharpens the base model's distribution over whole completions rather than retraining the model.
first_principles: The method upweights high-likelihood full sequences under a powered version of the base distribution and uses iterative MCMC-style resampling to approximate samples from that sharper distribution.
example: A base model generates an answer, then resamples blocks of the answer and keeps changes that better fit the sharpened likelihood landscape.
why_it_matters: It suggests that better decoding can recover much of the one-shot reasoning benefit of RL while preserving pass@k diversity.
misunderstanding: Power sampling is not the same as low temperature. Low temperature sharpens local token choices; power sampling tries to account for future completion likelihoods.

title: RL Information Inefficiency
plain_meaning: RL information inefficiency means RL often gives very little learning signal per unit of compute, especially on long tasks with sparse final rewards.
first_principles: Pretraining gives token-level feedback on every token. RL may generate thousands or millions of tokens before receiving one success/failure bit. If the pass rate is near zero or near one, even that bit carries little useful information.
example: A model works for an hour on a coding task and only learns that the final solution failed. It does not automatically know which step caused the failure.
why_it_matters: This explains why curriculum design, process rewards, verifiers, DAPO-style filtering, and task generation near the model's frontier are so important.
misunderstanding: RL being inefficient does not mean RL is useless. It means the reward bits are expensive and must be aimed carefully.

title: Algorithmic Progress Categories
plain_meaning: Algorithmic progress is not one thing. It mixes architecture, optimizers, systems work, data improvements, distillation, long-context methods, RL, tools, and evaluation design.
first_principles: If model performance improves at fixed compute, the cause could be a better learning algorithm, better data, better implementation, better hardware utilization, better inference strategy, or a new post-training paradigm. Lumping all of these together obscures what actually changed.
example: A newer model may beat an older model because it used better synthetic math data, not because its transformer block is fundamentally better.
why_it_matters: This matters for forecasting and engineering. The next bottleneck depends on which source of progress is actually driving gains.
misunderstanding: Calling everything algorithmic progress can double-count gains and hide the role of data and systems engineering.
